problem: Bounded Burnside problem: for which positive integers m, n is the free Burnside group B(m, n) finite? In particular, is B(2, 5) finite?
missing_details: Definition of B(m,n) as the quotient of the free group of rank m by the normal subgroup generated by all n-th powers of its elements
Specification that m denotes the number of generators and n denotes the (bounded) exponent of the group
Explanation that exponent n means every element satisfies g^n = 1
Universal mapping property: any group generated by m elements of exponent n is a homomorphic image of B(m,n)
Clarification that finiteness refers to the group having finite order
refined_question: Let m and n be positive integers. Define the free Burnside group B(m,n) as the quotient of the free group of rank m by the normal subgroup generated by all n-th powers of its elements; equivalently, B(m,n) is the (unique up to isomorphism) group on m generators in which every element satisfies g^n = 1 and which maps homomorphically onto any m-generator group of exponent n. For which pairs (m,n) is B(m,n) a finite group? In particular, does B(2,5) have finite order?
justification: The given name captures the core open question—determining finiteness of the free Burnside groups B(m,n) and the specific unresolved case (2,5)—but omits key definitions and context needed for a stand-alone statement, such as the construction of B(m,n), the meaning of exponent, and its universal property. These are enumerated in missing_details, hence a completeness score of 7.
